questions.question: Let $T\ge0$ be an absolutely continuous future lifetime with survivor $S(t)=P(T>t)$. At an elapsed duration $t>0$, assume $S(t)>0$ and $S$ is differentiable. For $h>0$, which quotient has limit $-S'(t)/S(t)$ for every such model as $h$ decreases to zero?

A life is currently aged $x=50$ years. Let $T_x$ be remaining lifetime and let $\mu_{x+t}$ denote the mortality force after elapsed duration $t\ge0$ years. Which force applies after three years of survival?

An absolutely continuous future lifetime has survivor $S(u)$. At one elapsed duration $t>0$, assume $S(t)>0$ and $S$ is differentiable. Its force satisfies $\mu(t)=0$ at that duration. Which conclusion must follow?
options: No deaths can occur at any later duration.
Everyone from the original cohort is still alive at that duration.
The survivor derivative is zero at that duration.
The survivor is constant throughout some surrounding interval.

questions.question: A continuous lifetime model has constant force of mortality 2 per year. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The rate is permissible; one-year death probability is $1-\mathrm{e}^{-2}$.
The model is invalid because the mortality force exceeds 1.
The one-year death probability is exactly 2.
The one-year survival probability is exactly $1/2$.

questions.question: A continuous lifetime model has a strictly increasing force $\mu(t)$ as elapsed duration $t$ rises. What does this describe?
options: A higher probability of survival to later durations.
A necessarily higher unconditional lifetime density at every later duration.
A higher proportion of the initial population alive at later durations.
A higher instantaneous death rate among those surviving to later durations.

questions.question: Future lifetime $T$ is uniform on $(0,5)$ years. At duration 5 its survivor is $S(5)=0$; one density version sets $f(5)=0.2$. What is its force at duration 5 under the positive-survivor definition?
options: $0.2$ per year, using the endpoint density.
$0$ per year, since no lives survive.
$+\infty$ per year, treating $0.2/0$ as the force.

questions.question: At elapsed duration 2 years, an absolutely continuous lifetime has survival probability $S(2)=0.7$ and mortality force $\mu(2)=0.03$ per year. Use the density version $f(t)=-S'(t)$ at differentiability points. What is $f(2)$?
A life has constant mortality force $0.04$ per year throughout the next year. What is its exact probability of death within that year?
Future lifetime $T$ has survivor function $S(t)=1/(1+t)^2$ for elapsed duration $t\ge0$ in years. What is its mortality force at $t=1$ year?
A mortality force at the current age is $0.06$ per year and is continuous nearby. Which is the first-order approximation to the probability of death during the next $h=0.01$ year?
A continuous lifetime model has mortality force $\mu(u)$ at elapsed duration $u\ge0$, and initial survival probability 1. For horizon $t>0$, which quantity determines its survival probability to $t$?

Let $S(t)=P(T>t)=\exp(-\int_0^t\mu(u)\,\mathrm{d}u)$, with $S(r)>0$ at $r>0$. For $h>0$, which expression for $P(T>r+h\mid T>r)$ is valid for every admissible mortality-force profile and all such $r,h$?

In a continuous lifetime model, survival to duration $a$ has positive probability. The mortality force is zero throughout $[a,b]$, where $b>a$. What follows about deaths between $a$ and $b$ among those alive at $a$?
options: The conditional probability of death in that interval is zero.
The conditional probability is positive because the interval has positive length.
The probability is determined by mortality before $a$.

questions.question: At elapsed duration $t\ge0$ years, a lifetime has mortality force $\mu(t)=0.02+0.01t$ per year. What is its probability of survival through the first two years?
A life alive now has constant mortality force $\lambda>0$ per year over the next two years. Its probability of death within those two years is 0.1. What is $\lambda$?

A continuous lifetime model has increasing mortality force $\mu(t)=2t$ for $t\ge0$ years and survival $S(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t^2}$. Use the density $f(t)=2t \mathrm{e}^{-t^2}$. At which positive duration does this density reach its maximum?
options: It keeps increasing at every positive duration.

questions.question: A proposed lifetime model starts with $S(0)=1$ and uses non-negative mortality force $\mu(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-t}$ for all elapsed durations $t\ge0$. It defines $S(t)=\exp(-\int_0^t\mu(u)\,\mathrm{d}u)$. If the lifetime must be finite with probability 1, what problem arises?
options: Positive force at every finite duration already guarantees eventual finite death.
Initial survival 1 already guarantees a finite lifetime distribution.
Force tending to zero makes the probability of no finite death equal to 1.
Its limiting survival is $\mathrm{e}^{-1}>0$, so it leaves positive probability of no finite death.

questions.question: Future lifetime has survivor $S(t)=\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$ for $t\ge0$ years. A density version equals $2\mathrm{e}^{-2t}$ except at $t=1$, where it is assigned the value 7. Define the mortality force at $t=1$ through $-\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\log S(t)$. What is that force?

Two lifetime models have force profiles in years: model A has $\mu_A(t)=0.2$ throughout; model B has $\mu_B(t)=0.1$ for $0\le t<0.5$, then $0.3$ for $0.5\le t<1$, and $0.2$ thereafter. Both start with survival 1. What do their survival probabilities at durations 0.5 and 1 show?
options: They agree at both durations because their one-year average forces agree.
They agree at 1 year, but model A has higher survival at 0.5 year.
They agree at 1 year, but model B has higher survival at 0.5 year.
Model B has lower survival at both durations because its later force is higher.

questions.question: Among lives currently alive, group A has proportion $0.4$ and constant mortality force $0.12$ per year; group B has proportion $0.6$ and constant force $0.02$ per month. A month is $1/12$ year, with no further selection within either group. What is the probability that a uniformly selected current life dies within the next month, to five decimal places?
